title: Labneh balls in olive oil
subtitle: Preserved strained yoghurt rolled in herbs and spice
excerpt: Labneh balls are small rounds of firm strained yoghurt, rolled in herbs and spices and then packed into a jar with olive oil. They keep for two weeks in the fridge and are one of the most useful things you can make from a pot of yoghurt.
sourceNotes: Claudia Roden, A Book of Middle Eastern Food (1968). Preserved labneh balls described as a Levantine pantry staple, made in batches and stored in olive oil. Anissa Helou, Lebanese Cuisine (1994). Detailed method for straining, rolling, and preserving labneh.

recipe.batchNotes: Double the yoghurt quantity to fill a larger jar. Keeps for two weeks in the fridge.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: The labneh needs to strain for at least 48 hours before rolling. Can strain for up to four days for a firmer result.

content.text: Labneh balls are strained yoghurt pressed into small rounds, rolled in dried herbs and spices, then packed into a jar of olive oil. They firm up over 48 hours of draining and keep for two weeks in the fridge. Serve them on bread, crumbled into salads, or alongside olives and flatbread.
You need a sieve lined with muslin or a clean tea towel and a bowl underneath for straining. A large jar with a lid for storing, sterilised with boiling water.
Mix {{sea-salt-fine}} into {{greek-yoghurt}} and stir to dissolve. Line a large sieve with muslin or two layers of clean J-cloth and set it over a deep bowl.
Tip the salted yoghurt into the lined sieve. Fold the cloth loosely over the top and refrigerate for 2 to 3 days. The whey will drip into the bowl below and the yoghurt will firm up considerably.
The finished labneh should be firm enough to roll into a ball without sticking to your hands. If it still feels sticky after 48 hours, leave it another day.
Mix {{za-atar}}, {{chilli-flakes}}, and {{sesame-seeds}} together on a small plate.
With lightly oiled hands, roll walnut-sized pieces of labneh into smooth balls. Roll each ball in the spice mix to coat all over.

Place the coated balls carefully into a sterilised jar. Pour {{extra-virgin-olive-oil}} over the top until the balls are fully covered. Seal and refrigerate. They are ready to eat after a few hours and are best within two weeks.

items.symptom: The labneh is too soft to roll after 48 hours
items.cause: Some full-fat yoghurts retain more liquid
items.fix: Leave for another 24 hours. The whey drains slowly and the labneh firms as it goes. It will get there.

items.symptom: The balls crack or collapse when rolling
items.cause: Hands too dry or labneh slightly too firm
items.fix: Lightly oil your palms before rolling. Work quickly and gently in small circular motions.

items.symptom: The spice coating falls off in the jar
items.cause: The balls were not pressed firmly enough into the coating
items.fix: Roll each ball several times and press lightly so the spices adhere. They will settle into the olive oil.

items.symptom: The olive oil solidifies in the fridge
items.cause: Olive oil firms up below around 7 degrees
items.fix: This is normal. Remove the jar from the fridge 20 minutes before serving so the oil returns to liquid.

content.text: Preserved labneh balls are a household staple across Lebanon, Syria, and Palestine, made in large batches at the end of summer when yoghurt was plentiful. Traditionally packed into clay jars with olive oil and left to mature over weeks, they were eaten through the winter months. Home cooks still make them, though the batches are smaller now. On a mezze table they sit beside olives, pickles, and fresh vegetables as part of the spread that appears before the main course. The herb and spice coating varies by household: some use dried thyme only, others mix in nigella seeds, dried chilli, or cumin.
